# Estimating density as a latent variable from two observation processes
## Packages
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
# multi-species
library(dclone) 
library(rjags) 
```

## Framework

Imagine we will sample birds during the morning (05:30-8:00) of every possible day at their breeding territory, and the birds defend that territory across the breeding season of that year. We can use point-counts and Passive Acoustic Monitoring in the same sites $m$. These two observation process should link with the ecological process (latent) of the abundance of individuals available to be detected and providing cues of their presence, which will be stationary during the sampling period (every morning during the breeding season). Evidently, some mornings and sampling events will have stochastic variation, reflecting a noise in the process that could be also accounted for. From empirical data, we have seeing that point counts are underdispersed (0 < Variance-to-Mean Ratio < 1), while acoustic detections are overdispersed (Variance-to-Mean Ration > 1).

```{r}
# Gompertz functions
gompertz <- function(t, K = 1, a = 5, b = 0.5) {
  K * exp(-a * exp(-b * t))
}

gompertz_decay <- function(t, K = 1, a = 5, b = 0.5) {
  K - gompertz(t, K, a, b)
}

# Time
t1 <- seq(0, 20, length.out = 200)
t2 <- seq(20, 40, length.out = 200)

# Deterministic mean curve
mu_vec <- c(
  gompertz(t1, K = 0.5, a = 5, b = 0.4),
  gompertz_decay(t2 - 20, K = 0.5, a = 5, b = 0.4)
)

# Add stochasticity (process noise)
set.seed(123)
sigma_proc <- 0.03
latent_stochastic <- mu_vec + rnorm(length(mu_vec), 0, sigma_proc)

# Sampling window
stationary_start <- 10
stationary_end   <- 22

# Sampling indices
sample_idx <- sample(120:150, size = 15)

acoustic_vec <- rep(NA, length(mu_vec))
counts_vec   <- rep(NA, length(mu_vec))

acoustic_vec[sample_idx] <- rnorm(15, mean = 0.65, sd = 0.5)
counts_vec[sample_idx]   <- rnorm(15, mean = 0.25, sd = 0.1)

df <- tibble(
  time     = c(t1, t2),
  mu       = mu_vec,
  latent   = latent_stochastic,
  acoustic = acoustic_vec,
  counts   = counts_vec
)

# Plot
ggplot(df, aes(time)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = latent, 
                color = "Latent",
                fill = "Latent",
                shape = "Latent"), 
            size = 1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mu, 
                color = "Mean",
                fill = "Mean",
                shape = "Mean"), 
            linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(y = acoustic, 
                 color = "Acoustic", 
                 fill = "Acoustic", 
                 shape = "Acoustic"), 
             size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = counts, 
                 color = "Counts", 
                 fill = "Counts", 
                 shape = "Counts"), 
             size = 2) +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = stationary_start, xmax = stationary_end,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#00000010", 
           color = "#00000020") +
  annotate("rect",
           xmin = 11, xmax = 16,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#ADD8E640", 
           color = "#ADD8E690") +
  annotate("text", x = 18, y = 0.71, label = "Breeding", color = "#00000040") +
  annotate("text", x = 14, y = 0.01, label = "Sampling", color = "#72bcd4") +
  annotate("text", x = c(4,28), y = 0.41, label = "Non-breeding", color = "#00000040") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = "gray50",
                                "Latent" = "black",
                                "Acoustic" = "#FFA500",
                                "Counts" = "#A020F0")) +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = "gray50",
                                "Latent" = "black",
                                "Acoustic" = "#FFA50060",
                                "Counts" = "#A020F060")) +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "",
                     values = c("Mean" = NA,
                                "Latent" = NA,
                                "Acoustic" = 24,
                                "Counts" = 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,30)) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Abundance") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.85,0.8),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank())
ggsave(filename = "figs/Framework.jpg")
```

![Framework for estimating latent density from two observation process using stochastic GSS](figs/Framework.jpg)

Here we want to estimate the latent abundance (black line of the figure) from two observation process: counts from point counts (purple downward triangles) and acoustic detections from passive acoustic monitoring (orange upward triangles). The figure is fake data, with the unique purpose of present our framework and ecological rationale.

## Ecological process

Let's assume that we have sites of sampling $m = 1,2,~...~,~M=10$ and species $s = 1,2,~...~,S = 4$ in an area. Our latent state $X_{t,m,s} = \log{(N_{m,s})}$ is the site-level log-abundance state for species $s$ at the site $m$, which follows a stationary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, OU, diffusion for Gompertz function dynamic on the log-scale across time $t$, which could be discrete units of 10-min duration:

$$
X_{t+1, m, s} = a_s + c_s * X_{t, m, s} + \epsilon_{t};\\ ~ \epsilon_t \sim \text{Normal}(0,\sigma_s^2)
$$

where $a_s$ control the drift (the initial condition at $t=1$, and then equivalent to the maximum growth rate in a population model), $c_s$ controls the mean-reverting dynamic (such as the strength of density dependence, $c_s = 1 + b_s$ in a population model), and $\epsilon_{t}$ captures stochasticity in the process, distributed as a normal random variable with some noise of the process as variance $\sigma_s^2$. Under stationarity and independence across sites, we can estimate the mean of the log-abundance as a function of the control drift and mean-reverting dynamic:

$$
\text{E}[X_{\infty, m, s}] = \mu_s= \frac{a_s}{1-c_s}
$$
This stationary value is represented as the dashed gray line tracking the latent dynamic (black line) in the framework figure during the sampling period.

We can also estimate the variance of this value:

$$
\text{Var}[X_{\infty, m, s}] = \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2}
$$

We can simulate a community by sampling $X_{t,m,s}$ i.i.d. (independent and identical distributed) across $m$ from this stationary distribution. Dealing with the Janzen's inequality, we can add half of the variance to the $\hat{\mu_s}$. The expected abundance per site $m$ of each species $s$ becomes:

$$
\text{E}[\lambda_{m,s}] = \exp \left( \mu_s + 0.5 \times \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2} \right)
$$

But to simulate observed data, we can initiate the time-series with the realized latent state at $t = 1$:
$$
X_{1,m,s} \sim \text{Normal} \left(\mu_s, \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2} \right) \\

\lambda_{1,m,s} = \exp(X_{1,m,s})
$$

and the temporal trajectory within a site across the sampling period (15 blocks of 10-minutes each morning, 05:30 to 07:50, for ten days,  $t = 1, ..., T_m = 150$) looks like: 

$$
X_{t+1, m, s} = a_s + c_sX_{t,m,s} + \epsilon_{s}, \\
\epsilon_{s} \sim \text{Normal}(0,\sigma^2_s)
$$
and each time has its own realized latent state:
$$
\lambda_{t,m,s} = \exp(X_{t,m,s})
$$

This latent state should be similar between the two observation processes $\lambda_{t,m,s}^{Counts} \approx \lambda_{t,m,s}^{Acoust}$. 

## Observation processes

In our thought experiment, we can conduct point counts in an approximated area of 0.78 ha, equivalent from a 50m fixed radius (see [Lopez et al. 2017](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12856)). The point-count observed counts are 
$$
Y_{t,m,s}^{Counts} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{t,m,s}^{Counts} \times \tau_{s})
$$ 
\noindent where $\tau_{s}$ ranges between 0 and 1, and is a species-specific detection probability. It could be reasonable to assume additional differences across site ($\tau_{m,s}$), but that would over complicates the model for now. Other models (Royle-Nichols, TTD, N-mixture, hierarchical distance, see [Fiss et al. 2017](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ecs2.4954)) also assume equal detection probability across individuals and visits.

On the other hand, the acoustic detection data are 
$$
Y_{m,s}^{Acoust} \sim \text{Negative Binomial}(r_s,~\pi_{m,s}) \\
\pi_{m,s} = \frac{r_s}{r_s+\lambda_{m,s}^{Acoust}}
$$
\noindent where $r_s$ is the overdispersion parameter and $\pi_{m,s}$ represents the success parameter.

Thus, during the breeding season (May-June) we have the possibility to sample each site 30 times between 05:00 and 09:50 for several mornings, including various visits per site (such as 10 to 50). These 10-min duration sampling events generate the point counts (Binomial) and acoustic detection count (Negative Binomial) data in a simultaneous design. To accelerate the simulation, let's use two days ($T_m = 30 \times 2 = 60$)

## Simulating some data

Define sites $M$ and species $S$
```{r}
set.seed(123)
M <- 15
S <- 4
T_max <- 60

visits <- sample(10:50, M, replace = TRUE) # visiting 2:10 was too few info
T_m <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))
  
for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    sample_idx <- sort(sample(1:T_max, size = visits[m], replace = FALSE))
    sample_vec <- rep(NA, T_max)
    sample_vec[sample_idx] <- 1
    T_m[,m,s] <- sample_vec
  }
}

```

### Species-level parameters

To get stable equilibrium density dynamics (when $t \rightarrow \infty$, the log abundance $x_t \rightarrow \mu$), the mean-reversing parameter should be $|c_s|<1$. When $0<c<1$, the log-abundance approaches to equilibrium directly. In contrast, when $-1<c<0$ the dynamic follows a damped oscillatory behavior (see [Ponciano et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tpb.2018.04.002)). A mean-reversing parameter $c = 1$ identify exponential dynamics. Based on our assumption that individuals already arrived to their territories, we could also assume that the mean-reversing is not leading to damped oscillatory behavior nor exponential dynamics, so ranging $0.1 < c < 0.9$. We can rely on the infinitesimal relationship $\theta = -\log(c)$.   

We know that the stationary mean log-abundance $\mu_s = \frac{a_s}{1-c_s}$. Thus, if we can "force" a mean log-abundance reasonable (such as between $\log(0.5)$ and $\log(10)$; see Fig 3 in [Fiss et al. 2017](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ecs2.4954)). Or also, use a $\log(\mu) \sim \text{Normal}(2,1)$.

With these two parameters, we can compute $a_s = \mu \times c_s$.

For the environmental stochasticity noise we can use the ranges reported in [Dennis et al. (2006)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/0012-9615%282006%2976%5B323%3AEDDPNA%5D2.0.CO%3B2) and/or [Dennis et al. (2017)](http://www.math.ualberta.ca/~slele/publications/Lele%20Dennis%20Lutscher%20data%20cloning%20Ecology%20Letters%2020071.pdf), $\sigma_s^2$ between $0.001$ and $0.3$. We can use $\log(\sigma^2) \sim \text{Normal}(0,1)$.

With these parameters, we can draw process $X_{t,m,s}$

```{r}
set.seed(123)
# for the OU latent variable, we can rely on 
lmu <- rnorm(S, log(3), 0.3)
ltheta <- rnorm(S, log(0.3), 0.2)
lsigsq <- rnorm(S, log(0.05), 0.3)

mu_s <- lmu             # mean stationary log-abundance
theta_s <- exp(ltheta)  # spead of equilibrium
sigsq_s <- exp(lsigsq)  # noise of environmental stochasticity

K_s <- exp(mu_s)        # mean stationary abundance
c_s <- exp(-theta_s)    # mean-reversion parameter
a_s <- mu_s * (1 - c_s) # control the drift 

var_statio_s <- sigsq_s / (1 - exp(-2 * theta_s))

X <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S)) 

for(s in 1:S){ 
  for(m in 1:M){
    # first visit, drawn from the stationary distribution
    X[1,m,s] <- rnorm(1, mean = mu_s[s], sd = sqrt(var_statio_s[s]))
    
    # OU recursion process moving throughout time
    for(t in 2:T_max){
      X[t,m,s] <- rnorm(1, mean = (a_s[s] + c_s[s]*X[t-1,m,s]), sd = sqrt(sigsq_s))
    }
  }
}

```

Expected density per species per site at each time of visit.
```{r}
lambda <- exp(X)
cool.palette <- as.vector(MetBrewer::met.brewer("Homer2",10))

jpeg("figs/Simulate_4s_10m_30t.jpeg", 
    width = 800, height = 900, units = "px", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(2,2),oma=c(5,5,4,1), mar=c(2,2,2,1))

for(s in 1:S){
  plot(1:T_max, lambda[,1,s], 
     pch=16, type="b",  bty="l",
     xlab="", ylab="", main = paste0("Species ", s),
     ylim=c(0,15), col=alpha(cool.palette[1], 0.5), cex.lab=1.15)
  for(m in 2:M){
    points(1:T_max, lambda[,m,s],
           pch = 16, type = "b", col = alpha(cool.palette[m], 0.5))
  }
}
mtext(text = "Latent expected abundance (30 sites)", side=2, outer=TRUE, cex=1.25,line=1)
mtext(text = "Time (60 10-min sampling in 2 days)", side=1, outer=TRUE, cex=1.25,line=1)
dev.off() 
```
![Simulated expected latent abundance of four species in 30 sites](figs/Simulate_4s_10m_30t.jpeg)

### Observation process by point counts

Recall:
$$
\lambda_{t,m,s} = \exp(X_{t,m,s}); \text{ Continuous}\\
n_{t,m,s} \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_{t,m,s}); \text{ Integer for Binomial} \\
Y_{t,m,s}^{Counts} \sim \text{Binomial}(\text{size} = n_{t,m,s};~ \text{p} =\tau_{s})
$$ 

We need the detection probability parameter $\tau_{s}$. We aim to underdispersion but not extreme, so moderate $\tau_s$ and not too much heterogeneity. Given our empirical data, we know that the counts are Binomial, so the mean is $np$, while the variance is $np(1-p)$, being $n$ the number of trials (size, true abundance with detection binomial) and $p$ is the detection probability ($tau$ in our case). Thus, $\text{VMR} = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{\text{E}(Y)} = \frac{np(1-p)}{np} = 1-p$. Although detection probabilities for North-American birds distributes with right-skew shape, we can use a beta distribution with shape1 = 6 and shape2 = 4 across species.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
# Species-level mean detectability 
tau_s <- rnorm(S, 0.5, 0.05)

Y_counts <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))

for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    for(t in 1:T_max){ 
      if(!is.na(T_m[t,m,s])){# only visited sites
        # point count Binomial detection
        lambda_obs <- round(lambda[t,m,s])
        Y_counts[t,m,s] <- rbinom(1,lambda_obs, tau_s[s])
      }
    }
  }
}

```

### Observation process by acoustic detections counts

Recall:
$$
Y_{t,m,s}^{Acoust} \sim \text{Negative Binomial}(r_s,~\pi_{t,m,s}), \\
\pi_{t,m,s} = \frac{r_s}{r_s + \lambda_{t,m,s}}
$$

We need the overdispersion parameter $r_s$. The variance for a Negative Binomial is $\text{Var}(Y) = (\lambda+\lambda^2)/r_s$, being $\lambda$ the expected value (mean $\text{E}(Y) = \lambda$). The Variance-to-Mean Ratio is $\text{VMR} = \frac{\text{Var}(Y)}{\text{E}(Y)} = \frac{\lambda + \frac{\lambda^2}{r_s}}{\lambda} = 1+\frac{\lambda}{r_s}$. Thus, $r_s = \frac{\lambda}{\text{VMR}-1}$.

Empirically, although the mean of acoustic detections counts in our dataset was 11.363 and the Variance-to-Mean Ratio mean 18.872, we do not need a value of $r_s\approx \frac{11.36}{18.87-1}\approx 0.64$, instead we can use the true lambda ($\bar{\lambda} = 3.46$; $r_s\approx \frac{3.46}{18.87-1}\approx 0.19$). The Gamma distribution with shape = 6 and rate 10 generates a mean $\approx 0.6$ generates 

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
r_s <- rnorm(S, 0.19, 0.01)

Y_acoust <- array(NA, dim = c(T_max, M, S))

for(s in 1:S){
  for(m in 1:M){
    for(t in 1:T_max){
      if(!is.na(T_m[t,m,s])){ #only visited
      pi_tms <- r_s[s] / (r_s[s] + lambda[t,m,s])
      Y_acoust[t,m,s] <- rnbinom(1, size = r_s[s], prob = pi_tms)
      }
    }
  }
}
```

ggsave(filename = "figs/Simulating_Latent_Observed.jpg",

# Remove NA values in the array of counts

## Fit a stochastic GSS model to recover the parameters

Let's prove if we can recover the parameters for one species, arbitrarily selected because underdispersion of counts and overdispersion of acoustic detection counts ($s=1$). We need a model that represent our stochastic GSS (OU) in a datacloning framework. First, select the species.

```{r}
sp1 <- 1

Yc_s <- Y_counts[ , , sp1]
Ya_s <- Y_acoust[ , , sp1]
# to mask visits (turning off the likelihood log(L) = 0)
visit <- ifelse(is.na(T_m[,,sp1]), 0, 1)
Yc_s[is.na(Yc_s)] <- 0 # this is not a problem because the matrix visit will indicate sampling times per site
```

### Fit model for counts (previous)

Let's fit first a "Counts" model

```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
CountOU.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(3), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
#  ltau ~ dnorm(log(0.3/(1-0.3)), 1/(0.5^2)) # logit-normal 
  
#  tau <- 1/(1+exp(-ltau))  # detection probability
  tau <- 0.5 #fixing tau close to true value to evaluate convergence and informability
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
  # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # point count Binomial detection
        N[t,m,k] ~ dpois(exp(X1[t,m,k])*visit[t,m,k])
        Y_counts[t,m,k] ~ dbin(tau, N[t,m,k])
      }
    }
  }
}

```

And we can bundle the data and fit the model with data cloning.
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# initialize some values
inits.c <- list(
  list(lmu=1.2,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8),
  list(lmu=1.8,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6)
  )

datalist.dc <- list( 
  K = 1, # clones start at 1 
  M = M, # number of sites 
  qp1 = T_max, # number of time steps 
  visit = dcdim(array(visit, dim = c(T_max,M,1))), #, # [t,m] → [t,m,k]
  Y_counts = dcdim(array(Yc_s, dim = c(T_max,M,1))) #, # [t,m] → [t,m,k]
  )

start_time <- Sys.time()
dcrun.GSS.c <- dc.fit(data = datalist.dc,
                    params = c("c", "a", "sigsq"), 
                   inits = inits.c,
                    model = CountOU.dc, 
                    n.clones = c(1,2,4,8,16),
                    multiply = "K",
                    unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
                    n.chains = 3,
                    n.adapt = 2000,
                    n.update = 5000,
                    thin = 10,
                    n.iter = 15000)

saveRDS(dcrun.GSS.c, "data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_count_tauFix.rds")

duration_model <- Sys.time()-start_time
print(duration_model)
```

This fit with $T_{max}=60$ had a duration of 59 minutes in my laptop (~4 hours in my old computer), longer than a previous attempt with $T_{max}=20$ but reducing process variance and reverting parameter biases.

After several trials, I have found that $\tau_s$ is unidentifiable and generate structural confounding with $\mu$, driving non-convergence of the model estimation. By fixing $\tau_s$, the model stabilizes. When trying a $\tau_s \neq \text{true}$, generates the parameters $\hat{a} = 0.36252 ~ [0.33009-0.3968]$, $\hat{c} = 0.64965 ~ [0.61736-0.6814]$, and $\hat{\sigma^2} = 0.01846 ~ [0.01526-0.0215]$, compared with the true values $a_1=0.2465564$, $c_1 = 0.7350194$, $\sigma_1^2 = 0.04068938$. When using $\tau_s^{\text{fixed}} = 0.5$, the MLEs where $\hat{a} = 0.14481 ~ [0.127762-0.16219]$, $\hat{c} = 0.83217 ~ [0.812466-0.85180]$, and $\hat{\sigma^2} = 0.01015 ~ [0.008957-0.01123]$. Thus, $c$ could be interpreted as robust to $\tau$ choice, suggesting that the temporal dependence is identified from dynamics, not detection scale. This also occur with the process variance $\sigma^2$. 

### Fit model for acoustic detection counts

Let's fit first a "Acoustic" model

```{r Stochastic GSS model for data cloning fitting of point counts}
AcoustOU.dc <- function() {

  # Priors (no cloning)
  lmu ~ dnorm(log(3), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  ltheta ~ dnorm(log(0.3), 1/(0.2^2)) # in precision terms
  lsigsq ~ dnorm(log(0.05), 1/(0.3^2)) # in precision terms
  r ~ dnorm(0.19, 1/(0.01^2)) 
  
  mu <- lmu
  theta <- exp(ltheta)
  sigsq <- exp(lsigsq)
  
  c <- exp(-theta)
  a <- mu * (1-c)
  Vinf <- sigsq/(1-exp(-2 * theta))
  
   # Likelihood (data cloning)
  for (k in 1:K) {               # K = clones
    for (m in 1:M) {             # M = sites
      
      # Stationary distribution for t=1
      X1[1,m,k] ~ dnorm(mu, 1 / Vinf) # JAGS works with precision

      # State process over time
      for (t in 2:qp1) {
        X1[t,m,k] ~ dnorm((a + c * X1[t-1,m,k]), 1 / sigsq) # JAGS works with precision
      }

      # Observation processes
      for (t in 1:qp1) {
        # Acoustic Negative Binomial detection
        pi_nb[t,m,k] <- r / (r + exp(X1[t,m,k]))
        Y_acoust[t,m,k] ~ dnegbin(pi_nb[t,m,k], r)
      }
    }
  }
}

```

And we can bundle the data and fit the model with data cloning.
```{r, eval=FALSE}
# initialize some values
inits.a <- list(
  list(lmu=1.2,  ltheta=-1.3, lsigsq=-3.1, r = 1.0),
  list(lmu=1.5,  ltheta=-1.1, lsigsq=-2.8, r = 2.0),
  list(lmu=1.8,  ltheta=-0.9, lsigsq=-2.6, r = 3.0)
  )

datalist.dc.a <- list( 
  K = 1, # clones start at 1 
  M = M, # number of sites 
  qp1 = T_max, # number of time steps 
  Y_acoust = dcdim(array(Ya_s, dim = c(T_max,M,1)))  # [t,m] → [t,m,k]
  )

start_time <- Sys.time()
dcrun.GSS.a <- dc.fit(data = datalist.dc.a,
                    params = c("c", "a", "sigsq", "r"), 
                   inits = inits.a,
                    model = AcoustOU.dc, 
                    n.clones = c(1,2,4,8,16),
                    multiply = "K",
                    unchanged = c("M","qp1"),
                    n.chains = 3,
                    n.adapt = 2000,
                    n.update = 5000,
                    thin = 10,
                    n.iter = 15000)

saveRDS(dcrun.GSS.a, "data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_acous.rds")

duration_model <- Sys.time()-start_time
print(duration_model)
```

This fit had a duration of 2.8 hrs in my computer. We can check the MLEs:

## Compare parameters from the two models

Call the results from the two models

```{r results of the data cloning fitted model point counts}
dcrun.GSS.c <- readRDS("data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_count_tauFix.rds")
dcrun.GSS.a <- readRDS("data/dcfitGSS_Sp1_upto16cl_acous.rds")
dcdiag(dcrun.GSS.c) 
plot(dcdiag(dcrun.GSS.c))
pairs(dcrun.GSS.c)
summary(dcrun.GSS.c);

dcdiag(dcrun.GSS.a) 
plot(dcdiag(dcrun.GSS.a))
pairs(dcrun.GSS.a)
summary(dcrun.GSS.a);
```

And we can put it in a single table
```{r}
MLEs_c <- summary(dcrun.GSS.c)$quantiles
MLEs_a <- summary(dcrun.GSS.a)$quantiles

idx_p <- match(rownames(MLEs_a), rownames(MLEs_c))

MLEs_c2 <- MLEs_c[idx_p,]

true_param <- c(a_s[1], c_s[1], r_s[1], sigsq_s[1])

tab <- tibble(
  param = rownames(MLEs_a),
  true = true_param,
  counts_25 = MLEs_c2[, "25%"],
  counts_50 = MLEs_c2[, "50%"],
  counts_75 = MLEs_c2[, "75%"],
  acoust_25 = MLEs_a[, "25%"],
  acoust_50 = MLEs_a[, "50%"],
  acoust_75 = MLEs_a[, "75%"]
)

tab
```

## Compare latent expected abundance

With the MLEs, we can reconstruct the OU trajectory:

$$
\hat{X}_{m,t} \sim \text{Normal}\left(\frac{\hat{a}}{1-\hat{c}}, \frac{\hat{\sigma^2}}{1-\hat{c}^2}\right); \\

\hat{\lambda}_{t,m} = \exp(\hat{X}_{t,m})
$$

and then compare the latent expected abundance
$$
\lambda_t^{(\text{counts})}=\exp(X_t^{(\text{counts})}) ~ \text{vs} ~ \lambda_t^{(\text{acoust})}=\exp(X_t^{(\text{acoust})})
$$

```{r}
a_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[1]
c_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[2]
sig_hat_c <- coef(dcrun.GSS.c)[3]

mu_hat_c <- a_hat_c / (1 - c_hat_c)
var_hat_c <- sig_hat_c / (1 - c_hat_c^2)

X_hat_c <- matrix(NA, nrow = T_max, ncol = M)

# Initialize from stationary distribution
X_hat_c[1,] <- rnorm(M, mu_hat_c, sqrt(var_hat_c))

# OU/Gompertz dynamics
for (t in 2:T_max){
  X_hat_c[t,] <- rnorm(M, (a_hat_c + c_hat_c * X_hat_c[t-1,]), sqrt(sig_hat_c))
}

lambda_c <- exp(X_hat_c)
```

```{r}
a_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[1]
c_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[2]
sig_hat_a <- coef(dcrun.GSS.a)[4]

mu_hat_a <- a_hat_a / (1 - c_hat_a)
var_hat_a <- sig_hat_a / (1 - c_hat_a^2)

X_hat_a <- matrix(NA, nrow = T_max, ncol = M)

# Initialize from stationary distribution
X_hat_a[1,] <- rnorm(M, mu_hat_a, sqrt(var_hat_a))

# OU/Gompertz dynamics
for (t in 2:T_max){
  X_hat_a[t,] <- rnorm(M, (a_hat_a + c_hat_a * X_hat_a[t-1,]), sqrt(sig_hat_a))
}

lambda_a <- exp(X_hat_a)
```

We can see the time series comparison for a single site
```{r}
matplot(1:T_max, cbind(lambda[, 1,1],lambda_c[, 1], lambda_a[, 1]),
        type = "l", lty = c(1,2,3), col = c("black", "red", "red"),
        ylim = c(0,6), ylab = "Expected abundance in site 1")
legend("topright", legend = c("True", "Counts", "Acoustic"), 
       col = c("black", "red","red"), lty = c(1,2,3))

```

Given the Janzen inequality, we can contrast also the stationary expectations

$$
\text{E}(\lambda) = \text{E}[\exp(X)] = \exp\left(\mu + 0.5 \frac{\sigma_s^2}{1-c_s^2}\right)
$$

```{r}
E_lambda <- exp(mu_s[1] + 0.5 * var_statio_s[1]) # for the species 1

E_lambda_c <- exp(mu_hat_c + 0.5 * var_hat_c)
E_lambda_a <- exp(mu_hat_a + 0.5 * var_hat_a)

E_lambda; E_lambda_c; E_lambda_a
```

A little off, but around the value! How many individuals off, on average? We can answer this by estimating the absolute bias
```{r}
bias_c <- mean(lambda_c) - lambda[,,1]
bias_a <- mean(lambda_a) - lambda[,,1]

mean(bias_c); mean(bias_a)
```

Across times and sites, the counts model underestimated abundance by 0.3 individuals on average, while the acoustic model underestimated abundance by 0.4 individuals on average.

```{r}
bias_c_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(bias_c)) |>
  mutate(time = as.numeric((Var1)),
         site = as.numeric((Var2))) |>
  rename(Counts = Freq)

bias_a_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(bias_a))|>
  mutate(time = as.numeric((Var1)),
         site = as.numeric((Var2))) |>
  rename(Acoustic = Freq)


bias_c_df |>
  left_join(bias_a_df) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Counts, Acoustic)) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, site, fill = value)) +
    facet_grid(~name)+
    geom_tile()+
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red")+
    labs(x = "Time", y = "Site", fill = "Bias")+
    theme_minimal()

```
